findings.problem: The consequence gloss states without qualification that the non-resident pharmacy's seven-business-day period starts earlier than the resident pharmacy's. That holds only where the improper dispensing is discovered before the serious injury or death is discovered, which is the ordinary case but not a necessary one: where a pharmacy learns of the patient's serious injury first and identifies the dispensing error afterwards, the 247 CMR 20.07(3) trigger falls later than the 247 CMR 20.02(1) trigger would.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 20.02(1) runs within seven business days of discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing, and 247 CMR 20.07(3) runs within seven business days of discovery of the improper dispensing. The regulations fix two different trigger events; neither is ordered ahead of the other as a matter of law. The defect is confined to an explanatory gloss: the same entry's own timeframe field states the 20.07(3) trigger correctly, and orientation[6], comparison_tables[2] row 'What starts the clock', retrieval_prompts[9], common_traps[12] and worked_examples[4] all state the distinction neutrally as a difference of trigger rather than of order. A candidate who applies the stated trigger reaches the right date on any Massachusetts facts, so the imprecision is a mnemonic overreach rather than a misstatement of the deadline.

findings.problem: Two derived fields compress the first sentence of 247 CMR 15.03(1) into a freestanding escalation duty borne by each member of pharmacy personnel: 'places the escalation duty on all pharmacy personnel' and 'The escalation duty under 247 CMR 15.03(1) sits on all pharmacy personnel, so a technician or clerk who holds an observation until a later shift has already missed it'. The regulation frames the sentence as a training requirement: all pharmacy personnel shall be trained to bring any QRE to the attention of the pharmacist on duty or the pharmacist Manager of Record immediately upon discovery.
findings.rationale: The duty-holder of 'shall be trained' is the pharmacy, and the content of the training is immediate escalation; the regulation does not in terms impose a separately enforceable obligation on the individual technician or clerk. The section is precise about this elsewhere and does not conceal it: orientation[1] and role_duties[0] reproduce 'shall be trained to' verbatim, and comparison_tables[0] row 1 expressly labels 15.03(1) a training and escalation duty. The behaviour the compressed fields instruct, escalating at once, is exactly what the regulation's training requires, so a candidate reading the section is not led to a wrong answer on Massachusetts facts; the imprecision is a teaching compression of the actor rather than a substitution of one legal actor for another.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 247 CMR 2.00, definitions of Pharmacy, Institutional Pharmacy and Manager of Record

results.summary: Verified every proposition in the section against the current official text and found it legally accurate within the scope it declares. 247 CMR 15.00 (12/6/24 edition) was checked in full: the six minimum provisions of 15.02(1)(a)-(f); the 15.03(1) escalation sentence and the three immediate items in (a)-(c), with the professional-judgment parenthetical attaching to the prescriber alone; the 24-hour clock in 15.03(2)(a) running from discovery by or description to the pharmacist; the four content elements of 15.03(2)(b)1.-4.; the three analysis elements of 15.03(3)(a)1.-3. and the Response half in 15.03(3)(b); and all four subsections of 15.04, including the two-year minimum measured from the date of the QRE report, the orderly-and-filed-by-date standard and the off-site storage permission. 247 CMR 20.00 was checked in full: 20.02(1) (Manager of Record, the Board, seven business days from discovery of serious injury or death related to improper dispensing); 20.02(2) (three recipients, the Board, the FDA MedWatch Program and the Betsy Lehman Center, and seven business days from knowledge by any pharmacy employee); 20.02(3)'s in-addition-to clause; 20.02(4) (all records relating to the event, a five-year minimum from the date the report is filed with the Board, readily retrievable); 20.02(5), quoted verbatim; 20.03(7) (the four Massachusetts pharmacy types, a copy of the Report of Theft or Loss of Controlled Substance and DEA Form 106 to the Board within seven days of the theft or significant loss, and the DEA, Department and state and local police clause); and 20.07(1)-(3), including the 20.07(3) trigger at discovery of the improper dispensing. 105 CMR 700.008 is reproduced verbatim and correctly routed to the Drug Control Program on its own form within 24 hours of discovery, with suspected tampering standing as an independent trigger; the 700.001 definition of Registrant, 700.004(A)(1)-(A)(3) (including Pharmacist at (A)(2)(f) and Health Facility at (A)(3)(d)), the four waiver findings in 700.140, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) (every pharmacy shall register with the said board) and the second paragraph of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 (dispenser: the local police department and the state police; distributor: the state police; simultaneous with the Form 106) all check out as stated. On the point the section flags for itself, it quotes 20.02(5) exactly, confines the carve-out to the reporting requirements in 20.02(1)-(3), reasons from 20.07(1)'s all-provisions-unless-otherwise-provided clause that the 20.02(4) records duty survives, expressly marks the contrary reading as available in orientation[7] and exceptions[9], and gives advice that complies under either reading. Every absolute word tested is supported: the professional-judgment qualifier is the only discretionary element in 15.03(1); 20.07 supplies a replacement only for the improper-dispensing report and none for a serious adverse drug event; and 247 CMR 15.00 as promulgated contains no confidentiality or privilege provision, which the section states in properly bounded terms. The section also reproduces each regulation's own actor language rather than generalising it, so nothing is claimed about pharmacy types the text does not reach. All nine listed practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted by it, including MA-Q-0369, whose community-pharmacy facts the section reconciles with the Department-registrant limit through 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2). Two Low imprecisions are recorded: an unqualified starts-earlier comparative in one timing consequence gloss, and a compression of 15.03(1)'s training duty into a personal escalation duty in two derived fields. Each is stated correctly elsewhere in the same section and neither would lead a candidate to a wrong answer on Massachusetts facts. One smaller wording looseness is noted here rather than as a finding: retrieval_prompts[7] calls the 15.04(4) off-site storage permission one of three things 15.04 requires, while the answer text itself correctly calls it a permission, as quick_review[17] does. The section is publishable to a candidate as it stands.
